#2654. MLB rumors: Max Scherzer mulling another season, Ty France drawing interest, top Taiwanese reliever posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Saturday's hot stove happenings.

Future Hall of Famer Max Scherzer will pitch in "lockout games" this offseason to determine whether he will continue his career, reports the New York Post. The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Players on opposing teams work out together throughout the offseason and figure to put together games to stay sharp during the lockout.

Scherzer, 42, made 18 starts around injuries with the Blue Jays this season. If 2026 was his final season, he went out with a bang. Scherzer struck out seven in seven innings of one-run ball in Game 162. He is currently ninth all-time with 3,557 strikeouts, three behind former Tigers teammate Justin Verlander. We did not rank Scherzer among our top 50 free agents.

Multiple teams have interest in free agent Ty France, according to The Athletic. A deal could come together quickly. France had a career year in 2026 after opening his stance a bit, which unlocked more hard-hit ability. He's a terrific defensive first baseman as well. We ranked France as the offseason's 23rd-best free agent, and the second-best available first baseman.

It's unclear which teams are in the hunt for France, though there is no shortage of contenders who could use the 32-year-old. The Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mets, Rangers, and of course Padres stand out as potential landing spots. Given his career year and the surprising lack of right-handed power in the game right now, France could command a multi-year contract

The Fubon Guardians of the Chinese Professional Baseball League have posted righty reliever Jyun-Yue Tseng for MLB teams, reports the Associated Press. Officially, Tseng has until Dec. 22 to sign, though the expected lockout means his signing deadline is really Dec. 1. We did not rank him among our top 50 free agents.

Tseng, 25, pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026. He saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings this past season. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s but has run as high as 100 mph in the past. His secondary pitches need work to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2652. Miami Heat to host 2028 NBA All-Star Weekend, first time since 1990, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Miami is one of the sports world's most beloved event hosts. Super Bowls and National Championship Games are frequently held in South Florida, but for quite some time, the NBA's marquee regular-season event has been held elsewhere. The Miami Heat hosted All-Star Weekend in 1990, their second season in existence, but haven't hosted it since.

Well, that's about to change. Miami will host the event in 2028, after Phoenix does so in 2027, according to ESPN. The decision comes on the heels of widespread complaints about All-Star Weekends being held in smaller, less desirable cities to visit.

In 2024, The Oklahoman, questioning why Oklahoma City was not hosting the event, reported that the NBA planned to start enforcing minimums on certain amenities for prospective All-Star markets, including at least 7,250 hotel rooms and three five-star hotels, at least 650,000 square feet of convention center and exhibition space, and at least 75 nonstop domestic flights and at least 20 international flights. The NBA denied that these were ironclad requirements. Miami is the second city to earn an All-Star Weekend since that report, joining Phoenix, as San Francisco (2025) and Los Angeles (2026) were already settled. All four cities are notably relatively warm in February.

So, why did it take so long for Miami in particular to get a second All-Star Weekend? The answer may be the Miami International Boat Show, which occupies much of the city's hotel and convention space capacity and usually comes during Presidents' Day weekend, which often conflicts with the NBA's All-Star schedule. However, the Boat Show will reportedly be moving to a different weekend in 2028 to accommodate the NBA, which will hold All-Star Weekend from Feb. 18-20.

The Heat did not put in a bid to host All-Star Weekend, according to the Miami Herald, and have typically avoided doing so in the past. Instead, the NBA reportedly approached the Heat about hosting, and now, Miami will get its first All-Star Game in almost four decades.

#2650. Predicting full 14-team NFL playoff bracket after trade deadline: Entire NFC North makes postseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL trade deadline was Tuesday, and no one made a bigger move than the Minnesota Vikings. With their season hanging in the balance, the Vikings decided to make a trade for Kirk Cousins.

Thanks to the move, the Vikings are expected to coast into the playoffs along with EVERY OTHER TEAM in the NFC North. That's right, in our latest projection, we have all four NFC North teams making the postseason. If that happens, it would mark the first time in NFL history that a division has sent all four of its teams to the playoffs in one season.

So who else is projected to get in? Glad you asked.

To help us figure that out, we had our analytics expert, Stephen Oh, simulate the rest of the 2026 season. There are 136 games left on the regular-season schedule, along with 13 playoff games, and Oh simulated all of them. Not only did he project all eight division winners and the 14 playoff teams, but he also crowned a Super Bowl champion.

With that in mind, let's get to the projections. And just as a reminder, we're projecting what the NFL playoff field will look like at the end of the season. This is NOT the current playoff standings.

The AFC playoff picture is starting to take shape, and based on our projection, it's starting to feel like the playoff teams in this conference are almost locked in at this point. For the second straight week, not only does our projection have the same seven teams making the playoffs, but they're all seeded in the exact same spot.

Here's the projected AFC playoff field (with each team's current record):  1. Bills (7-1) -- AFC East champion 2. Jaguars (6-2) -- AFC South champion 3. Broncos (7-2) -- AFC West champion 4. Bengals (6-2) -- AFC North champion 5. Chiefs (6-2) 6. Steelers (6-2) 7. Patriots (5-4) JUST MISSED: Texans (3-5), Browns (5-4)

According to our projection, the only real battle will be for the seventh seed. We have the Patriots projected to get the spot right now, but the Texans are nipping at their heels. We have both teams projected to finish the season at 9-8, but the Patriots are sneaking in thanks to a better conference record.

The good news for the Vikings is that adding Kirk Cousins does help: They're now projected to finish with 11 wins — compared to 10 without Cousins — but the problem is that 11 wins won't help them win the division. According to our projection, the Vikings are going to finish THIRD in the NFC North, but that will still be enough to get them in the postseason.

Here's the projected NFC playoff field (with each team's current record):  1. 49ers (7-1) -- NFC West champion 2. Lions (6-2) -- NFC North champion 3. Giants (5-2-1) -- NFC East champion 4. Buccaneers (3-6) -- NFC South champion 5. Bears (7-2) 6. Vikings (6-2) 7. Packers (6-3)  JUST MISSED: Seahawks (5-4), Rams (5-4)

For the first time all season, our model is projecting ALL FOUR NFC North teams to make the playoffs. At this point, it feels like the only way that's not going to happen is if the Rams or Seahawks get to 11 wins, but our computer doesn't see that happening.

Having all four teams from a single division make the postseason in the same year wasn't possible until 2020, when the NFL expanded the playoffs to 14 teams. Since then, there have been several instances where a division has put three teams in, but we still haven't seen a division put all four of its teams in, so this could be a history-making season.

AFC breakdown: Homefield advantage ends up being an actual advantage here, with all three home teams winning in the opening round. With the Patriots and Chiefs going out, they would eliminate the two teams that have represented the AFC in eight of the past nine Super Bowls.

NFC breakdown: The NFC North has been the best division in football all year, and the division makes a statement in the wild-card round by producing three winners. If this happens, we'd get a rarity: The NFC North would become just the fifth division in NFL history to send three teams to the divisional round.

AFC breakdown: If our projection proves correct, earning home-field advantage could be a big deal in the AFC. After watching the home teams sweep through the wild-card round, the run continues with Buffalo and Jacksonville both winning at home. With the win, the Bills advance to their third AFC title game since 2020 while the Jaguars make a return trip to the AFC Championship for the first time since 2017.

NFC breakdown: The Lions beat an NFC North team in the wild-card round, and they continue their postseason run by beating another NFC North team in the divisional round. As for the 49ers, Kyle Shanahan figures out a way to get his offense going against Minnesota's tough defense, propelling his team to a win. This sets up a rematch of the 2023 NFC title game between the Lions and 49ers.

If you're scoring at home, we are now down to four teams: Three teams that have never won a Super Bowl (Bills, Jaguars and Lions) and one team that hasn't won a Super Bowl in over 30 years (the 49ers' last title came in 1994)

We've been doing a projection every week since the start of the season, and here's a look at the projected Super Bowl each week.

As you can see, the computer has really taken a liking to the Bills, as this marks the third straight week Buffalo is projected to win the Super Bowl. Scratch that, the computer actually loves the Bills: Buffalo has a 16.94% chance of winning it all, which is a huge number when you consider there's only one other team that's even above 10% (the Jaguars are at 10.74%).

#2649. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2648. Where the WSL-chasing women’s team fit in ‘Newcastle United 2.0’

They are blazing a trail for a remodelled Newcastle United: top of WSL2, unbeaten in the league, pushing for promotion, brimming with ambition and, this weekend, facing second-place Sunderland in a north-east derby fixture which is being billed locally as "El Lassico". At a club where change has been a constant companion since their Saudi-led takeover five years ago, Tanya Oxtoby and her Newcastle team are demonstrating how it can be done.

In her office at the women's team training ground at Cochrane Park, Grace Williams shoots back. The director of football for Newcastle's women's side had been asked where they fit under the heading "Newcastle 2.0," which is how David Hopkinson, the chief executive, described the next stage of the club's development, in an interview with The Athletic in August. "It's not under, it's alongside," she says.

This clarification is important. The Premier League dominates in England and beyond — discourse, publicity, hyperbole, money — but Newcastle now have a formalised mission statement and top of the code is "One club. We are all in." The men's and women's teams have their own context and requirements, but in terms of attitudes and status, there is no substantive differentiation between the two.

As Hopkinson puts it: "The only way to view Newcastle United Women is as part of Newcastle. It's not a bolt-on. If it's a bolt-on, then it can wither. It's a huge part of our mandate and our mission."

The women's team were a passion project for Amanda Staveley, the financier who drove through the takeover and then part-owned the club. Having previously operated under the club's charitable foundation, they were brought into Newcastle proper, securing consecutive promotions up into the second tier under Becky Langley's management, going full time and fully professional. Back when it all started, players paid to play and juggled other jobs. Langley washed their kit.

Newcastle's growth was phenomenal, but Langley left last year, a couple of months after Williams was appointed, and was replaced by Oxtoby, who had most recently managed Northern Ireland and had spent two seasons as assistant coach to Emma Hayes at Chelsea. Her recruitment was led by Williams, but involved Hopkinson, Ross Williams, the sporting director, Jack Ross, who is now assistant sporting director, and James Bunce, director of performance. All in.

In the summer window, they signed 11 new players and their squad is crammed with senior internationals. They have moved training grounds, they are playing seven games at St James' Park this season and the rest at Gateshead International Stadium and everything is geared to going up and then progressing. If it is a less homely, less wide-eyed club, it is also bigger and more integrated. This is their era of meaning business.

After seven games in WSL2, Newcastle have won six and drawn one, giving them a three-point lead over Sunderland. "We're not counting any chickens," Hopkinson says, which is probably wise given that only one side is guaranteed automatic promotion. But they got their transfers done early and are reaping the benefit of preparation and gelling. "Really strong performances, great physical dominance; it's been a really exciting start for us," says Williams.

For the record, Hopkinson's searing timetable for Newcastle to be in the conversation for major honours applies here, too. "When it's presented to our people internally or to the investment community or to sponsors, it's all on the same slide," he says. "There aren't two slides here. Our ambition is to consistently and credibly compete for the top prizes in global football, for the Premier League and the WSL, by 2030."

"You could argue the pressure is a little bit different because we have to get into the top league first," Williams says. "We can't be competing at the top level until we get there and that means the expectation on us first and foremost is to be promoted.

"But we haven't shied away from that; we're very open and ambitious about it with our players and staff. That's what we need to achieve and then, as we aim towards 2030, it's about starting to compete at the top of the game."

In part, this explains the calibre of their signings. Although they are not there yet, Newcastle are looking ahead. "It's widely known and accepted that when you get promoted you often go from being an in-possession to an out-of-possession team," says Williams. In other words, winning sides tend to win a little less. "I definitely don't want us to change," she says. "We've tried to create a recruitment strategy for playing how we want to play."

"There was a big pull towards Newcastle for me with the ambition they have and the goals they're setting out," says Martha Thomas, the Scotland striker, who has played in the WSL with Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur, Manchester United and West Ham United. "I didn't want to join somewhere that was just staying steady. I wanted to join a club that was pushing on and backing the women's team completely."

Thomas, 30, has already scored nine goals in all competitions this season. While she will not be drawn into stating that Newcastle are a WSL club in all but name — "this is only the beginning and it's important we don't get complacent," she says — becoming one in practice is why she is here. "We've got the facilities, we've got the backing of the club, we've got the players, we've got the squad, we've got the coaching staff and all those things," she says.

At her other clubs, Williams has done it all, starting or restarting women's programmes. Her own start came at Watford, the team she supported as a child, "managing staff, managing a budget, running a football department, going into commercial pitches and also taking the kit home for my mum to wash," she says. "I got my hands dirty in every element of it. I'm sure I annoyed everybody at Watford, constantly asking, 'How do I do this, how do I do that'?"

Watford were promoted to WSL2. Bristol City, her second posting, were promoted to the WSL, as were Crystal Palace, her third. So what does it take?

"It's the golden question," she says. "I would never disregard all the other elements that come into it, but at the centre of it all is culture, the people who are around, the players, the coaches, everybody. What attracted me to Newcastle was that sense of, 'We want to be in the WSL and here's how we think we can do it'.

"There was a really strong ambition to support women's football, a care about the players and the game and how we can make an impact. They want to improve what women's football looks like in the North East. That was a really important box ticked for me. And they had already taken steps.

"For me, it was a good opportunity not going in to start from scratch. It was adding the structure and strategy behind it."

The one-club element is not just for show. Jack Ross spends a day a week at the women's base, just as he does at the men's academy. Bunce has direct responsibility for the performance element of the women's team. And when they were a coach down after Langley's departure, it was Ross's idea not to make an external appointment but to approach Peter Ramage, the former defender, who is talent management lead at the club.

"Peter didn't even think about it," Williams says. "It was, 'Yes, I love the club, how can I support, how can I help?'. Then there was a bit of, 'My god, I've never worked in women's football before', but he was great. It was a brilliant opportunity to bring the club together organically. Peter still comes in to see us once a week. Our coaches go over to the academy building to learn from them. It's something I've never experienced before."

"I talk a lot about alignment, but this is what I mean," Hopkinson says. "We're all going in the same direction. You can't have one club as one of your core values and then have an invisible asterisk alongside it that says 'Yeah, but not the women. They're on an island'. One club needs to be inclusive; it needs to be everybody included in our thinking, our priorities and in our strategies. And they are."

On the same theme, Oxtoby got together with Matthias Jaissle, her counterpart with the men's team, not too long ago, to swap ideas and experiences. "They met, had a coffee and shared some best practice," Williams says. "They both know the door is open and hopefully that will continue and they're able to get to each other's games. Tanya knowing that she has someone else to bounce off or speak to is great. And it's valuable for the club."

Oxtoby, says Thomas, has forged "a winning culture. There are non-negotiables: do everything to prepare, take it game-by-game, don't ever get too far ahead of ourselves, don't ever look too much into the past. She's very ambitious; she wants energy, she wants to bring out the best in us and create a strong team philosophy. She wants to win." Sunderland will be a test, but Newcastle have become pretty good at it.

Newcastle 2.0 is serving them well but the blueprint of what this team should look like is not unfamiliar. "I want us to be on the ball or fighting for every single ball," Williams says. "Front-foot, high-pressing, high intensity and we should train how we play. I love it when we win a throw-in and we get cheers from the crowd; I've never seen or heard that at other clubs.

"I want to see that fight and that grit in all our players and our staff."

This article originally appeared in The Athletic.

Newcastle United, Women's Soccer, Women's Super League

#2647. Champions Classic NBA Draft guide: Who scouts will be watching in college basketball's high-profile showcase

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The most anticipated double-header of the young college basketball season takes place tonight in Chicago as No. 2 Duke meets No. 5 Michigan State, followed by No. 15 Kansas vs. No. 24 Kentucky in the Champions Classic.

The event is also expected to draw a heavy dose of NBA scouts and decision-makers to Chicago, given the opportunity to see so many high-level prospects under one roof on one night.

One wrinkle: The best NBA prospect on the court Tuesday night won't even be eligible to be drafted in 2027. That's Duke freshman Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje who is 17 years old and won't turn 18 until next May. In order to be eligible for the NBA Draft, a player must be at least 19 years old during the calendar year of the draft, per NBA rules.

So not only will Boumtje Boumtje be ineligible for the upcoming draft; he is expected back at Duke for his sophomore season.

Another thing to keep in mind is that these NBA scouts and executives will use what they see on Tuesday night as a benchmark and something to measure against for the rest of the season. They will not over-index on what they see on just one given night.

The public, on the other hand, has a tendency to fall for that trap. Because tonight is so visible, if someone has a glaring performance (good or bad), it often anchors a lot of the public discourse for the rest of the season. Trevor Keels is the classic example. He scored 25 points in the 2021 Champions Classic, was mocked as a lottery pick almost immediately afterwards, ended up declaring for the draft prematurely, and slipped to the second round.

The moral of the story – keep what you see on Tuesday night in perspective, because the people who make the big decisions certainly will.

So with all that in mind, here's a look at the top NBA prospects from the four teams in action at the Champions Classic

This shouldn't come as a surprise, but the Blue Devils lead the way in terms of total NBA prospects. What's interesting about this year's team though, is that their best prospect, Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje, isn't even eligible this year, but is the early favorite to be the top pick in 2028. Boumtje Boumtje has a combination of size and skill, which is unmatched for his age, not just in college basketball, but anywhere in the world.

Ngongba had a chance to be a first-round pick a year ago, but opted to return to Duke, and so far, it looks a decision that is going to pay off. Ngonba fits a coveted NBA archetype in that he's a mismatch five-man who can play inside and out. He is a vertical spacer, reliable passer, and consistent offensive rebounder who has massive length to also be a rim protector. Scouts want to see him take the next step as a shot-blocker and as a rebounder while proving his durability.

If Ngongba can prove he can space the floor with his shooting, that's just an added bonus. He's prepared for that challenge by getting himself into the best shape of his career and looks poised to be the focal point for the Blue Devils, at least on the interior, this season. In short, it's early, but the lottery is very much in play here.

Sarr is a long and athletic big wing who, last year as a freshman, was already one of the best perimeter defenders in the ACC, if not the country. This year, he's going to get the volume to show his offensive growth. So far, that's come more in transition and as a secondary playmaker, but what the NBA is going to be most interested in is his ability to make spot-up 3s in order to fit that coveted 3-and-D archetype. Sarr was 32% from that range last season, but hasn't even attempted a three through two games this year, but has gotten to the free-throw line in high volume and made 71%, after connecting on only 53% last year.

While the progression of Sarr's total game is important, scouts will be monitoring the shooting most closely all year long. Duke also appears to be recruiting as if they expect Sarr to move on after the year. The first-round should be the expectation, with the late lottery not being out of the question.

Williams has quickly become one of the most polarizing draft prospects in the country. He was a top five recruit out of the high school ranks a year ago because of his combination of size, athleticism, fluidity, skill, and shot-blocking potential, even with real questions about his physicality.

Williams has played a limited role to start the season and could fall further out of the rotation as games get closer. Nevertheless, it wouldn't be at all surprising to see him explore professional opportunities, even if this season doesn't go as expected. It also wouldn't be unprecedented to see a team invest a first-round pick in trying to develop his tools, even in that scenario. It's a trajectory that could mirror that of Peyton Watson, who was a prized 2021 recruit who didn't play much in his freshman season at UCLA, still declared for the draft, and ended up being the 30th pick for the Nuggets a year later. That pick has gone down as a very good one.

If the exhibition slate was any indication, Blackwell may be Duke's most reliable player this season. He came to Durham after putting up 19 points and 5 rebounds on 43/39/86 shooting last year for Wisconsin, but did not get any first-round traction in the pre-draft process.

The narrative once Blackwell hit the portal was that he wanted to play with the ball in his hands. Fortunately, he seems to have gotten over that, because his path to the NBA is based on proving he can be a reliable two-way role player, not an alpha creator. Duke is the biggest stage to prove that. If the shooting splits hold up and he can provide some secondary playmaking and be a defensive asset, then hopefully scouts won't be so worried about his lack of length come the next draft cycle.

NBA scouts are also watching: Deron Rippey Jr., 6-1, freshman, guard; Bryson Howard, 6-4, freshman, guard; Caleb Foster, 6-4, senior, guard; Cayden Boozer, 6-3, sophomore, guard.

The Spartans are unlike many of college basketball's other top programs in that while they are projected to be among the very best teams in the sport, but they don't have as many glaring NBA prospects. Of course, similar claims used to be made about Villanova teams of old, and that proved to be beyond shortsighted, so it's possible that time will prove the masses wrong about the individual talent on this year's team.

Fears is undoubtedly one of the best players and floor generals in all of college basketball. Everything Michigan State does begins with him, and the same was true last year for a team that won 27 games and advanced to the Sweet 16 before running into UConn. There are, however, questions about how his game translates to the NBA. He lacks ideal measurables for the league, doesn't have the outlier burst to compensate, and is also a questionable shooter.

Still, it's hard to bet against Fears' will, and so chances are he figures out how to stick at the next level. The elephant in the room, though, is that while he is a true senior this year at Michigan State, his earning potential will almost certainly be higher in college than the pros next year. The Spartans have recruited as if he's not going to be back, but if and when financial reality hits, will they be willing to tolerate seeing him in another uniform? Only time will tell.

The baby-faced sophomore is still a work in progress and just starting to grow into his body and fill out his frame. Right now, he is much more of a Robin to Fears' Batman for the Spartans. And yet, Scott has a game that could ultimately translate to the next level more seamlessly. He's a big wing with positional size, a reliable floor-spacer who made 37% of his threes last year as a freshman. He's also a reliable decision-maker who turned the ball over a total of 32 times in 729 minutes a year ago. In short, the NBA is intrigued, so whether or not it's this year or down the road, Scott is on the right trajectory.

NBA scouts are also watching: Coen Carr, 6-6, senior, forward; Jasiah Jervis, 6-4, freshman, guard; Ethan Taylor, 7-2, freshman, center.

For the second consecutive year, Bill Self has a freshman with a chance to prove he should be the top pick in the draft. The biggest question for most of the summer, though, was based on who else they could get to surround Tyran Stokes. Now, thanks to eligibility being granted to Melvin Council, Tre White, and Tre Kaufman-Renn, the Jayhawks suddenly have an ideal supporting cast. Here's the thing, though: if those guys were NBA players at this point, they wouldn't have been available to return.

Stokes is the early favorite to be the top pick in the 2027 NBA draft. He's built like a throwback power forward, but can initiate like a guard, not just for himself, but for others as well. The biggest questions in high school were about his approach and ability to impact winning on a daily basis, but so far at Kansas, he's gotten rave reviews. Being surrounded by veterans no doubt helps, as does having some reinforcements. When Stokes dropped 27 points, eight rebounds, and seven assists on Duke in an exhibition, it was a sign of things to come. That performance came without the Jayhawks having yet established an ideal scheme to get him going in space and movement. In short, if Stokes' mindset stays the same, he has a chance to distance himself from the field this season, and that process could begin tonight.

NBA scouts are also watching: Taylen Kinney, 6-2, freshman, guard; Keanu Dawes, 6-9, senior, forward; Melvin Council Jr, 6-4, graduate, guard; Tre White, 6-6, graduate, wing; Trey Kaufman-Renn, 6-8, graduate, center/forward.

Malachi Moreno and Milan Momcilovic both had a good chance to be drafted last June. So, when they opted to return, it wasn't for a lack of options; it was for the valuation that college basketball, and Kentucky in particular, was able to pay them. That's a very different calculus than graduate students who return after not signing NBA contracts. So, while this year's roster may not have any glaring lottery picks, it does have pro talent.

Moreno fits a coveted archetype in today's NBA because he has legit size and can be reliable in offensive structure. He's a quick processor of the game and a reliable decision-maker at various spots on the floor. He's a solid passer, efficient finisher, and may even have some long-term shooting potential. He also provides some defensive rim protection, but could certainly help his stock this season by becoming more assertive around the rim on both ends of the floor. The first-round should be the goal for Moreno coming out of this season.

Momcilovic was one of the best shooters in college basketball last year, making 49% of his threes on almost 8 attempts per game, while also making 88% of his free throws for good measure. Through two games at Kentucky, he's getting even more volume, with 17 attempted threes in just two games so far. While his floor-spacing gravity is not in doubt, the questions for the next level are more about his ability to defend his position without putting his team in rotation. So, all-year scouts will be locked in on some of the nuances of Momcilovic's game, like his foot speed, angles, and rotations. Long-term, Momcilovic has positional size and a translatable niche, but may be in a familiar spot in the off-season, with more guaranteed money in the college ranks.

Wilkins was one of the best mid-major freshmen in the country last year, posting nearly 18 points and 5 assists for a Furman that went to the NCAA Tournament. He's a classic late-bloomer who had an undeveloped, wiry frame in high school, but quickly started to put things together as he grew into his body.

While he's still filling out, Wilkins is naturally smooth with real playmaking genes. Through two games at Kentucky, there's also been an early uptick in his shooting (he's 5-for-11 from three and 6-for-6 from the free-throw line). If that growth is sustainable, he'll continue to build momentum with NBA decision-makers. Exactly what his timeline will be, though, still remains to be seen.

NBA scouts are also watching: Kam Williams, 6-7, junior, wing; Zoom Diallo, 6-5, junior, guard; Mason Williams, 6-2, freshman, guard

#2645. MLB rumors: Why the Dodgers could be Tarik Skubal or bust; Red Sox looking for pitching depth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.

#2644. NFL Week 10 upset alert: Why the red-hot Bengals are in danger on 'Sunday Night Football'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It was a bad week to be an underdog in the NFL. Over the course of the Week 9 slate, favorites went 14-1 straight-up, with the lone upset coming from the Packers as they took down the Patriots in Foxborough.

Naturally, with favorites dominating the day, it wasn't a banner showing from us in last week's column. That said, we did correctly pinpoint New England as a prime upset candidate to Green Bay, so we'll take the win when we can get it.

With favorites finding so much success last week, however, it should heighten their concern heading into Week 10, as the pendulum could swing in the other direction to even things up. And there are several games to choose from this weekend for potential upsets, including a "Sunday Night Football" showdown between two AFC North rivals. So, let's get right to it and identify five favorites who are on upset alert.

The last time these two NFC East rivals faced one another, it was a calamity that resulted in a 27-27 tie. That said, I do think Washington is catching New York at the right time in this Thursday night matchup to begin Week 10.

Giants starter J.J. McCarthy was in and out of the lineup last week after suffering a hip pointer injury against the Eagles, but is expected to play in this game. Before going down, McCarthy seemed more like his Minnesota self than the quarterback who completed 20-of-28 in a win over the Texans before their bye. McCarthy threw for 127 yards on 12-of-19 passing in the win over Philly, with his yards per attempt (6.7) taking a noticeable dip from his first two appearances. He also took five sacks.

If that continues on Thursday against a Commanders defense that is allowing just 15.0 points per game over the past two games, Washington's offense may not have to do too much heavy lifting. Meanwhile, Jayden Daniels has largely had success against New York, coming into this game with a 3-0-1 record against his division foe. He's also totaled five touchdowns and zero turnovers in those games. Daniels has largely protected the ball this season as well and has yet to throw an interception.

So, the recipe for Washington here is for Daniels to keep a clean sheet in the turnover margin, and for McCarthy to come back down to earth.

Maybe a trip across the Atlantic snaps the Patriots back into form after an abysmal loss to the Packers at home in Week 9. One of the biggest issues for New England's offense this season has been turnovers, committing one on 19.4% of drives. While that's hardly going to instill much confidence in anyone backing the Patriots in Week 10, it is worth noting that Detroit hasn't exactly been known to create turnovers on defense. Entering this international game in Germany, the Lions have eight turnovers this season, which is tied for the fourth-fewest in the NFL. When you compare that to Green Bay's 19 total turnovers (second-best), the Patriots should get some reprieve in that department.

Meanwhile, Jared Goff hasn't looked as lights-out as he did over the first five games of the season when he was an early MVP candidate. Even amid this winning streak, Goff's numbers have dipped.

He's still playing at a high level, but it's not otherworldly, which could help New England's defense -- particularly the secondary -- put together a bounce-back performance.

Minnesota has the disadvantage of being on the road against a division rival and being on a short week after playing on Monday night, but they do get a huge boost on offense for this game. Before Tuesday's trade deadline, the Vikings pulled off a trade to acquire Kirk Cousins from the Raiders, which should elevate the offense to a more respectable level.

Coming into the week and pre-Cousins, Minnesota ranks 31st in passing yards per game (160.8) and is tied with the winless Chargers for the fewest offensive touchdowns (11) in the NFL this season. Despite all that, they're 6-2, which is thanks to their top-flight defense. Now that they have an offense that can not only complement them, but sustain drives to give them more rest on the sideline, Minnesota should be taken more seriously.

The defense will have its hands full against Green Bay's prolific passing attack, but they do have the personnel to contain them. That's especially true in the aftermath of Josh Jacobs (broken finger) being ruled out for this game, further limiting an already anemic ground game.

The Packers have also struggled in this spot. The club is 1-5 in its past six games against division opponents (including playoffs) and are 1-8 in its last nine games against teams entering the matchup four or more games over .500.

With the shot in the arm on offense with Cousins' arrival, the Vikings are live at Lambeau.

Carolina is in the midst of a three-game losing streak, which has brought Bryce Young's play into focus. Over the last three games, the Panthers quarterback has averaged 216 passing yards per game, has five passing touchdowns and four interceptions. While that's not great, context is key. Young and the Panthers have squared off against the Buccaneers, Packers (road), and Broncos during the skid, all of which are among the top defenses in the league right now. New Orleans is not that.

The Saints secondary has allowed 7.3 yards per attempt so far this season (tied for the fifth-highest in the league) along with a 99.5 passer rating allowed (seventh-highest). Meanwhile, Young was solid last week, albeit in defeat. He completed 71.7% of his throws for 276 yards, three touchdowns and a pick. That output should hold up against a weaker defense in New Orleans and should help propel them to snap the losing streak.

That's especially true considering the Saints haven't been a strong team at home so far in 2026. At the Superdome, they are 1-4 and have yet to cover (0-5 ATS).

Whoever constructed the schedule this year did the Bengals dirty for this Week 10 matchup. Not only are they returning from an international game in Madrid last week, but they are hosting a Steelers club that was on the bye in Week 9. That's a massive rest disadvantage for Cincinnati, which could rear its head in this matchup.

So far, Joe Burrow has been the talk of the NFL as he's leaped to the top of the MVP conversation after a sensational run over the Bengals' four-game winning streak. He has the offense averaging over 35 points per game and has 18 total touchdowns with a 132.0 passer rating. While those are video-game-like numbers, the competition he's been slicing up hasn't exactly been the Legion of Boom. Over the streak, Cincinnati has beaten up on the Dolphins, Ravens (no Lamar Jackson), Titans and Falcons.

The Steelers pose a much tougher challenge, especially on defense. Pittsburgh is tied for the fifth-lowest yards per play average (5.0), tied for the fourth-lowest points per game allowed (18.0), and tied for the eighth-lowest passer rating allowed (83.3).

Since 2020, the Steelers have also won and covered in each of their six games coming off the bye.

#2643. Re-grading the Jaylen Brown-Paul George trade: Celtics' grade has greatly improved, 76ers' mark stays perfect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Besides the Luka Dončić stunner, you could argue that this summer's Jaylen Brown blockbuster was the most surprising trade in recent NBA history. A former Finals MVP coming off of his best season traded for ... Paul George? Someone widely treated as one of the NBA's worst contracts and half of the draft capital a superstar typically fetches? The reactions were, obviously, extreme. Celtics fans revolted. Pundits expected a meaningful drop-off for Boston. Trade graders like myself pilloried Brad Stevens and his front office for moving a 29-year-old All-NBA forward for what appeared to be far less than fair value.

And yet, as Brown prepares to face his former employer for the first time, the two teams sit neck-and-neck in the Eastern Conference. The 76ers top the standings at 9-2. The Celtics are right behind them at 8-2, but have the East's best net rating at +11.6. While Philadelphia has thus far gotten exactly what it wanted out of the trade, the Celtics seemingly have as well. So with their first of potentially many high-stakes clashes this season set for Tuesday night (8 p.m. ET, NBC/fubo), let's revisit the trade and hand out revised grades for the offseason's most impactful trade.

The backlash to the George-for-Brown trade was fundamentally centered on two premises:

The first premise was, frankly, outdated in the apron era. Yes, Kevin Durant netted four first-round picks, a first-round swap, and players who would go on to net six additional first-round picks and another swap, but that was all the way back in February 2023, and that trade completely derailed Phoenix's future. The James Harden trade played out similarly for the Nets. Teams are more skittish about all-in moves for older players than they've ever been.

There have been outlier, extremely high-cost trades since then, but all came under somewhat irreplicable circumstances. Mikal Bridges netted five first-round picks and a swap, for instance, but he never misses games, came with two years of cheap cost-control and played collegiately with several other key Knicks. New York viewed him as the finishing piece of a championship team, and the Knicks were ultimately proven correct.

Desmond Bane wasn't as underpaid, but he fit the extremely narrow niche the Magic needed: someone who could enhance their offense without commanding high usage on a team that was already locked into two max-salary shot-creators or compromising their defensive identity. There were maybe a handful of players in the NBA Orlando could have targeted for that role, and Bane, amazingly, was probably the only one available. In an extremely injured Eastern Conference, the Magic tried to be opportunistic. That's where these lopsided trades happen. They're almost always circumstantial.

The more typical star trade scenario is something closer to what the Milwaukee Bucks went through with Giannis Antetokounmpo. The player is older, attempts to fix things internally have failed, and the relationship between star and team is no longer tenable. The acquiring team typically has a leverage advantage, and that's especially true in the apron era, where paying the sort of giant salaries these stars get in their early 30s carries far more risk than reward. Antetokounmpo netted three picks, one swap and a handful of players that won't be foundational for the Bucks. We know Antetokounmpo had more trade value than Brown because the Celtics tried to trade Brown and more for Antetokounmpo, but a deal wasn't struck. So if Antetokounmpo, a two-time MVP, was worth three-and-a-half picks plus some player value, Brown being worth two picks and some player value feels in line with the new, cost-conscious NBA.

And then of course, there's the matter of what the player value actually was. That brings us to George. From November through January of last season, George averaged just 16 points on 42-38-86 shooting. This was in line with his 2024-25 performance, and together, the year-and-a-half sample felt reliable for an aging star. Well, George then got suspended 25 games. When he returned in March, he was a 21-point scorer on better shooting splits who looked rejuvenated defensively. He went on to torch the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs. Most of us expected George to look more like the player he was before that suspension in Boston. The Celtics bet that he would look like who he was after, and thus far, they've looked correct.

The raw numbers are superb: 20.4 points, 47-43-81 shooting and his highest assist and rebounding rates since he left the Clippers. The fit has been even better. Much was made of how low many advanced metrics are on Brown relative to his reputation, but the more significant story here was always his outlier status within Boston's intended team structure. Joe Mazzulla wants to maximize 3-point attempt rate. George's 3-point attempt rate so far this season (51.4%) is nearly twice Brown's (27.8%). Brad Stevens spoke openly about not wanting to concentrate usage in two players, and George's usage rate is nearly eight percentage points lower than Brown's was a year ago. The Celtics wanted this sort of player in their system and next to Jayson Tatum, and it's working.

Yet just as vitally, George is helping the Celtics diversify a bit as a team. The Celtics generated the second-fewest turnovers in the NBA last season. They're averaging the eighth-most in the NBA thus far this season, and George is the single biggest reason why. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections, and among players who have played at least four games, only Daniels and Kris Dunn are generating more steals.

The Celtics had the lowest free-throw attempt rate in the NBA last season as well. They're right around the middle of the pack this year. Tatum is the one drawing most of those fouls, but George is a critical part of the structure that gets Tatum to the line. Brown can be a bit of a ball-stopper. Among true forwards, only Kawhi Leonard and Zion Williamson averaged more seconds per touch than Brown a year ago. The average George touch this season lasts 3.3 seconds compared to just under five for Brown a year ago. It's simply easier to compromise a defense when the ball is moving and players are making quick decisions. That's how defenses are forced into rotation and wind up fouling out of desperation. As a team, the Celtics have the sixth-lowest average time per touch this season compared to the eighth-highest a year ago.

Even the contract feels a bit more palatable now than it did at the time. Brown would have become eligible for an extension on his supermax contract last offseason, and based on the season he had, he would have been more than justified in asking for one. The Celtics, clearly, had no plans to commit extra years to Brown on top of the three that he was already owed. George isn't quite living up to his supermax price tag thus far this season, but his deal is a year shorter and comes with no such extension pressure.

If anything, his player option for next season opens some interesting doors for the Celtics if they decide they're happy with this partnership. As of right now, the Celtics have around $3 million in first-apron room for the 2027-28 season based on current projections. Say they want to use the full mid-level exception on a free agent or perhaps need a bit more wiggle room to make a trade. They could theoretically go to George and ask him to lower his cap figure in exchange for another year of security. Turning a one-year, $56.6 million deal into, say, a two-year, $90 million deal could make sense for both sides provided George sustains this level of play.

The reasonable fear that he might not is why we stop at a "B-" for Boston. This is still his age-36 season. George has been injury-prone for most of his career. He presumably will not get a 25-game break this season, and even if he's this good all year, all of these benefits he's brought to Boston are somewhat regular-season-centric. The playoffs are a different game, one that leans much more into Brown's strengths as an individual shotmaker and man-to-man defender. The Celtics still never get to the rim. Their best answer for opposing star guards is probably Jordan Walsh, whose offense makes him hard to play for too long. If Boston flames out in the playoffs, we might view Brown's absence as one of the bigger reasons why. The path to actually winning this trade gets paved in April and May.

But for now, at least, it's starting to make sense. The Celtics added two premium draft assets in a way that allowed them to maintain their existing playing style and avoid taking a major step back in the present. They sidestepped what probably would have been an ugly contract negotiation, and the more barbs get traded in the press, the clearer it becomes that this situation simply was not salvageable. The Celtics had to trade Brown. The offers were far lower than we anticipated. Boston still managed to make the best of less-than-ideal circumstances and still factors prominently into the Eastern Conference championship picture.

Funnily enough, you could pretty easily argue that George would actually be a far better fit for this iteration of the 76ers than Brown is. Philadelphia's 20th-ranked offense has a bottom-five 3-point attempt rate and the eighth-highest average seconds per touch in the NBA. The Sixers could stand to trade some of that dribbling for a bit more shooting. Considering how lethal their transition offense can be, George's turnover generation would also fit this defense like a glove. The 76ers will get better offensively. We're still in tiny-sample season, and everyone's still learning how to play together. But George is undeniably the easier player to fit onto a roster like this than Brown.

Of course, the 76ers wouldn't have a roster like this without Brown. Widespread reporting has made it clear that Philadelphia's acquisition of Brown was what first caught the attention of LeBron James in free agency. If Brown was indeed a swing factor in the 76ers getting LeBron, that assuages any short-term salary concerns for Brown. For God's sake, the Philadelphia 76ers have LeBron James on a minimum contract. Even if Brown is overpaid, the surplus value on the James contract more than offsets any negative value there.

The 76ers have far less reason to fear an extension than Boston did as well. By trading Brown, the Celtics subjected him to the NBA's six-month extend-and-trade restrictions. That meant he could only tack one year onto his contract rather than two, and because he has multiple years remaining on his contract, he's not eligible to extend during the season. The 76ers therefore get to table those discussions until the offseason at the earliest, and remember, at that point, Brown will be negotiating off of the more modest statistics that come with sacrificing for the sake of a superteam. It's simply easier to envision Brown extending at less than the max in Philadelphia than it would have been in Boston.

Speaking of sacrificing, remember the whole "Jaylen Brown wants his own team" narrative from last offseason? For all we know, it was true at the time and might have remained true had he stayed with the Celtics. So far, that has been a complete non-issue for the 76ers. Brown is currently sporting his lowest usage rate since 2020 (before he became an All-Star). He's turning the ball over around half as often per 100 possessions as he did a season ago. He's an enormous part of a defense that surprisingly ranks No. 6 in the NBA so far this season. He's even openly called the 76ers Tyrese Maxey's team.

And the 76ers are, obviously, winning. They're mostly winning clutch games, but hey, you expect to win close games with four stars in your starting lineup. They're going to figure out the finer points of maximizing this talent mix over time, but even the "getting to know each other" version of this group poses almost impossible matchup problems for other teams. Take Cleveland, who has already faced Philadelphia twice. Can you guess which two Cavalier defenders have spent the most partial possessions guarding Brown, per NBA.com tracking data? James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, at 60.6 combined. Those are the sort of defenders you try to hide on weak scorers to preserve for offense. Well, where exactly are Harden and Mitchell supposed to hide against this team? There are no weak spots. The advantage of having this many creators is that Philadelphia basically starts every possession with an exploitable mismatch.

On pure talent accumulation alone, this is the sort of roster teams tend to go all-in for. Philadelphia didn't even have to. While the Stepien Rule complicates the tradability of some of their remaining picks, the 76ers are still slated to have four first-round picks in the next seven drafts. There is still ammunition for some sort of pivot here, whether that's a short-term upgrade to maximize this title run or more likely, some sort of long-term change at center as Joel Embiid gets older and potentially less reliable from a health perspective.

There are going to be depth questions down the line. Even if Brown gets less than a 35% max on his eventual extension, he's going to be pricey. Maxey feels like a near-lock for a supermax extension in the years to come, and while VJ Edgecombe will almost certainly be limited to 25% of the cap on his rookie extension, he'll still account for quite a bit of money. The 76ers are a top-heavy roster today, and that's after hitting a few home runs on the margins and getting arguably the greatest player of all time to take the minimum. Sustaining contention beyond the "Embiid is still a matchup nightmare and LeBron is on the team" era is going to require near-perfect management on the margins.

But this isn't rocket science. How many teams have a trio they can feel better about for, say, the next three-to-five years than Maxey, Brown and Edgecombe? The Brown trade opened an immediate championship window and likely ensured a relatively high baseline for the rest of the decade, assuming acceptable health and wise decisions elsewhere on the roster. It was a great trade in July and it remains a great trade today.

#2642. MLB rumors: Why the Cubs may already be out on Tarik Skubal, plus latest on Phillies, Cardinals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

The expectation remains that we'll see some level of activity on the trade and free agency fronts before the lockout begins in early December. As noted above, that was indeed the case leading up to the last lockout, and this time around, the prospect of drastic changes in the next CBA may have big-spending teams looking to fortify their rosters before those changes are implemented. Speaking of which, MLB Network reports that we could see some notable transactions go down at the upcoming General Managers Meetings, which take place from Nov. 10-12 in Las Vegas.

During a standard offseason, not much beyond behind-the-scenes groundwork goes down during the GM Meetings, and the real moves start happening at the December Winter Meetings. However, unless the lockout is resolved quickly – highly unlikely – then there probably won't be a Winter Meetings this offseason. That means the GM Meetings could be more active than usual.

Free agent ace and, until later this week, reigning back-to-back  American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is the prize of the offseason. The 29-year-old lefty is a fit for any of MLB's 30 teams, but heretofore the most serious bidders have been expected to be the Los Angeles Dodgers (who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers leading up to last season's trade deadline), the New York Mets, and the Chicago Cubs. Now, though, perhaps you can reduce that number of serious bidders to two. While Chicago very much needs rotation help for 2027 and beyond, the Athletic reports that the Cubs "are expected to stay on the sidelines" when the Skubal bidding gets serious. That, no doubt, will come as a disappointment to Cubs fans who are still waiting for the Ricketts to invest in the payroll at levels befitting a big-market contender.

The Cardinals traded away veteran lefty reliever JoJo Romero, along with starter and fellow free agent Dustin May, to the Milwaukee Brewers leading up to the trade deadline. Now, St. Louis may be interested in bringing Romero back on a free agent contract, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports.

Romero, 30, is coming off a 2026 season in which he pitched to a 3.36 ERA with a 3.00 K/BB ratio in 55 appearances. In the postseason with Milwaukee, Romero had a 1.13 ERA with 11 strikeouts and one walk in eight innings. He previously spent parts of five seasons with the Cardinals.

Do the Philadelphia Phillies need a new shortstop? That's one of the principal questions of their offseason. Although incumbent Trea Turner is signed through 2033, his defense at the crucial position of shortstop has degraded into "unplayable" territory, and that has the Phils considering fallback options should Turner need to be moved off the position. One option is free agent 31-year-old Ha-Seong Kim, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports. Kim, 32, spent last season on a one-year deal with the division-rival Atlanta Braves. He's been a primary shortstop for five of his six MLB seasons, and while he's certainly not among the very best at the position, he does profile as a major defensive upgrade over Turner. As for the bat, Kim for his career has an OPS+ of 93, and he's capable of stealing a base on occasion. He was, however, an offensive sinkhole for 51 games in 2026. Turner, meantime, may be looking at a switch to the outfield starting next season as the Phillies attempt to keep their contending window open.

#2640. Are Chelsea toothless without Lauren James? This is what the numbers say

First, 20 shots at Everton. Next, 32 shots at BK Hacken. Of the 52 shots in total across 180 minutes of football in four days, one finds the back of the net.

And if you square the eight and move the two and subtract the total of the square root of Ellie Carpenter's 20 crosses into the box, you'll find that the answer to the question that you're really asking — which is why things aren't straightforward for Chelsea when Lauren James isn't on the pitch — is actually quite simple. It's because Lauren James isn't on the pitch.

That was the diagnosis from many after Chelsea's consecutive stalemates, both of which James was absent from due to a hamstring injury sustained during a 6-0 win over Charlton Athletic at the start of the month that, according to the club, will see her out for multiple weeks.

It's not a terribly misinformed diagnosis. In terms of the 25-year-old England forward's skill set, there are few in the world like her. It lends a hand in explaining why it can look and feel so difficult for Chelsea without her.

It's worth noting that despite last season's notable underperformance in front of goal, Chelsea are scoring goals this season. They sit top of the WSL rankings for goals scored (28), shots (215) and the number of goalscorers (13).

Even so, they're still underperforming their xG (29.8) by -1.8, ranking second-from-bottom in the league for overall xG performance. As Chelsea host league leaders and reigning league champions Manchester City (two points ahead of Chelsea) on Saturday, a key narrative will be the absence of Chelsea's biggest threat.

As one rival analyst for a WSL club, speaking anonymously to protect relationships, put it, there is a sense of two Chelseas: Chelsea with James, and Chelsea without James. How congruously the statistics stack up to that claim is fascinating.

Since James' move to Chelsea from Manchester United ahead of the 2021-22 season, she has played 68 WSL matches (Opta does not provide data for FA Cup, League Cup or the Women's Champions League). Within those, Chelsea have recorded 54 wins, seven draws and seven losses, while averaging 18.6 shots with 37 per cent accuracy, 2.2xG, and 2.6 goals scored per game.

In the 51 matches James has missed (mostly due to injury), Chelsea have recorded 42 wins, six draws and three losses, while averaging 19.5 shots with 36 per cent accuracy, 2.5xG and 2.9 goals scored per game.

Meanwhile, Chelsea's conversion rate with James rests at 14 per cent, and 15 per cent without her (albeit in 17 fewer matches).

Numbers cannot quantify the feel of a match, nor does the above account for the share of creative and goalscoring responsibilities spread across different squads and changes of managers, or the number of matches James has been forced to miss due to injury.

It's worth considering James' overall numbers on a per-90 basis in the past four seasons and their context.

Since the 2023-24 season, James has managed more than 900 minutes of league football in two seasons: 2023-24 and 2025-26. Her 2023-24 season (the last of Chelsea's Emma Hayes era) was her best in a Chelsea shirt, managing 13 goals and two assists across 16 WSL appearances (16 goals and three assists across 29 appearances in all competitions).

Since then, James has been switched more gradually to the left (see the graphic below) while also taking on more creative responsibilities, dropping deeper to help build play.

Even so, other than the 2024-25 season (Sonia Bompastor's first season as Chelsea head coach, in which James managed just 562 minutes across nine WSL appearances), James has also overperformed her xG in every season since 2023-24, which speaks to the unrivalled quality of her finishing. And over the past two seasons, it's this sharpness which Chelsea have so drastically missed during her absences.

Since the start of last season, Chelsea have scored 24 goals from 31.4xG (a -7.4 underperformance) in the 12 games she has missed.

In the 19 matches James has featured in, they have scored 48 goals from 44.1xG (a +3.9 overperformance). Her five goals and four assists from 14 league games and 11 starts last season represented the second-highest volume of goal involvements in Bompastor's squad behind Alyssa Thompson (10), and were only bettered by 13 players in the league. James also ranked 14th in the WSL for key passes, despite her lengthy absence.

In her five WSL appearances this season, James has scored four goals (joint-second most for Chelsea) from an xG of just 2.2 (the sixth-best in the team).

Meanwhile, in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 seasons, Chelsea scored 90 times from 70.0xG in 34 games with James (a +20.0 overperformance) and 47 from 34.3xG (+12.8 overperformance) in 10 games without her. The latter is inflated a bit by two 8-0 wins and two 6-0 wins, but even when removing those, Chelsea scored 19 goals from 15.5xG in six matches (a +3.5 overperformance).

While James has missed more football in the time since the 2022-23 and 2023-24 seasons, what has also changed is how much responsibility James bears for Chelsea's creative and goalscoring output.

In the 2022-23 season, Sam Kerr, Guro Reiten, Pernille Harder and Fran Kirby all scored more than James' five goals.

In the 2023-24 season, in which James played the second-highest number of minutes in her Chelsea career behind the 2022-23 season, James ranked highest in the team for goals scored with 13. Still, Aggie Beever-Jones' 11 goals, along with eight from Sjoeke Nusken and seven from Reiten, helped to supplement that tally. In fact, that Chelsea squad boasted 19 goalscorers in total, with nine players managing more than two goals.

Last season, no Chelsea player managed more than seven goals, a culmination of underperformance as well as an injury-ravaged strike force. It was James' late return to the pitch that helped Chelsea to not only claim the League Cup but also secure Champions League football.

Despite Chelsea being held to a 1-1 draw against Aston Villa on the WSL's opening weekend, it was James' goal that opened the scoring and her moments on the ball which gave Chelsea their best chances. Her deployment as a false nine in September's 5-0 thrashing of Manchester United (in which she registered one goal) saw Chelsea at their ruthless best. In fact, in Chelsea's opening two matches, James registered 19 shots in total — a league record.

"We know how good Lauren is for us, for the team," Bompastor said after Chelsea's recent victory over Charlton. "My job is to make sure I find solutions when LJ isn't available. I looked at some of the statistics from last week and the good thing is we're a team who can score with different players."

Chelsea's attacking quality even without James shouldn't be underrated. The recent return to fitness of Japan forward Manaka Matsukubo will be a welcome boon. Bompastor's evolution of defensive midfielder Keira Walsh into a more creative outlet has also been fruitful. In the WSL, Walsh sits joint-top for goal involvements in Chelsea's squad with four assists and two goals alongside summer signing Melvine Malard, who has six goals. Walsh's two goals are only bettered by Ellie Carpenter and James (four each).

But reliability is needed from the front line and other areas of the pitch so the attacking onus doesn't fall onto a player who, at her best in a Chelsea shirt, has played 60 per cent of a season. For Bompastor and Chelsea, it could be what the season's success turns on.
